match: Add or extend automated tests for existing code, such as a function, a fallback path or an edge case, without changing that code's behaviour

fit.q: Does the request ask for new or extended automated tests?
Is writing tests the main work the request asks for, rather than a change to how the code behaves?

requires.q: Is the file described in `target.usage` itself an automated test file, rather than the code being tested?

escalate.q: To choose which cases to test, does an engineer first need to understand branching or fallback logic inside the code under test?

subject.q: Which candidate names the function, script or code path that the new tests cover?

items.text: Add automated tests that pin down the current behaviour of `{subject}`, without changing the code of `{subject}`.
`{target_path}`: {target_summary}. `{subject}` is defined there; its current behaviour is what the tests pin down.
The code under test lives in `{target_path}`; that file stays unchanged.
Existing tests for `{subject}` live in `{test_file}`; extend them rather than starting a parallel file.

guards.q: Does the request or `target.usage` name a specific test file, test suite or test group that already runs this code?

items.text: `{subject}` has no automated tests today; the new tests are its first coverage.

guards.q: Does the request or `target.usage` name a specific test file, test suite or test group that already runs this code?

items.text: When done: {desired}.
All new tests pass against the unchanged code of `{subject}`.
Each new test fails if the behaviour of `{subject}` that it covers changes.
Before writing tests, read `{subject}` end to end and list its observable behaviours: return values, output, exit codes, errors raised, and side effects on files or the environment.
Read the existing tests nearest to `{subject}` and copy their framework, helpers, fixture setup, file naming and assertion style; use only tools those tests already use.
List the branches of `{subject}` the request asks to cover and, for each, the smallest input or environment that makes it run; write one test per entry in that list.

For each fallback or error path, choose how the test forces it: an argument, an environment variable, a stubbed dependency, a missing file, or a restricted `PATH`. Prefer the mechanism the existing tests already use. Criteria: the test controls the condition fully and leaves no state behind.

guards.q: Does the request ask to test a fallback, error or failure path that runs only when something is missing or fails?

items.text: Decide how each fallback test proves which path ran, not only that the result looks right: a distinct output, a log line, a stub that records its calls, or a value only that path produces.

guards.q: Does the request ask to test a fallback, error or failure path that runs only when something is missing or fails?

items.text: For each edge case, run `{subject}` on it once by hand and record today's exact result; the test asserts that result, not a guess about the intended one.

guards.q: Does the request name edge-case inputs such as empty, missing, very large, malformed or boundary values?

items.text: List every external dependency `{subject}` touches (other programs, network, clock, file system, environment variables) and decide for each whether the test stubs it, points it at a temporary location, or uses it for real.

guards.q: Does the code under test call other programs, the network, the clock, or read and write files?

items.text: Each behaviour named in the request has at least one test whose name states which behaviour it covers.
Each test asserts a specific value, output, error or exit code; a test that only checks that the code runs without crashing does not count.
Tests cover both the primary path and the fallback path, so a regression that makes the fallback run every time is also caught.

guards.q: Does the request ask to test a fallback, error or failure path that runs only when something is missing or fails?

items.text: Each edge case the request names is its own test case (or its own row in a table-driven test), so a failure identifies the case.

guards.q: Does the request name edge-case inputs such as empty, missing, very large, malformed or boundary values?

items.text: Each new test passes when run alone and in any order with the others; it does not depend on state left by another test.
Temporary files, directories, environment changes and stubs live in a per-test temporary location and are removed or restored when the test ends, including when it fails.

guards.q: Does the code under test call other programs, the network, the clock, or read and write files?

items.text: No test reaches the network or a real external service; those calls are replaced by stubs or local fixtures.

guards.q: Does the code under test call the network or an external service?

items.text: Tests do not depend on the current time, random values, locale or machine-specific paths unless the test fixes them itself.
`{test_cmd}` runs the new tests without extra flags; if the runner lists test files explicitly, register the new file there.

items.input: a test that forces the fallback path of `{subject}` by removing the dependency it normally uses
items.output: the test asserts the fallback's result and that the fallback, not the primary path, produced it
items.reasoning: If the primary path gives the same answer, a test that checks only the result passes without ever reaching the fallback.

guards.q: Does the request ask to test a fallback, error or failure path that runs only when something is missing or fails?

items.input: an empty or boundary input to `{subject}`
items.output: the test asserts the exact result, error or exit code today's code produces for that input
items.reasoning: The tests pin down current behaviour; asserting an imagined intended result turns a test task into a behaviour change.

guards.q: Does the request name edge-case inputs such as empty, missing, very large, malformed or boundary values?

items.input: a new test shows `{subject}` returning a result that looks wrong
items.output: the code of `{subject}` stays unchanged; the test is skipped or marked as an expected failure using the project's mechanism, or left out; the report gives the input, the actual result and why it looks wrong
items.reasoning: Fixing the code is out of scope, and asserting the wrong result as correct would lock the bug in.

items.input: the behaviour a new test covers is deliberately broken inside `{subject}`
items.output: at least one new test fails, naming the broken behaviour
items.reasoning: A test that still passes when the code is broken gives no protection.

items.text: `{test_cmd}` exits 0 and its output lists the new tests as run and passed.
Before starting, copy `{target_path}` to a temporary file; at the end, `cmp <copy> {target_path}` exits 0.

For each new test, temporarily break the behaviour it covers in `{subject}` (for example invert a condition or change a returned value), run the new tests and confirm that one fails; then restore the file with `git checkout -- <file>` and confirm `git diff --quiet -- <file>` exits 0.
Run the new tests three times in a row: every run passes with the same results.
After the test run, `git status --porcelain` lists only the new or changed test files, fixtures and test helpers, with no production file and no leftover temporary files.
`{lint_cmd}` reports no new findings in the changed test files.
Add the new tests here, next to the existing coverage for `{subject}`, following that file's structure.

guards.q: Does the request or `target.usage` name a specific test file, test suite or test group that already runs this code?

items.text: Do not modify the code of `{subject}` or any other production code; only test files, fixtures and test helpers change.
Do not weaken, skip or delete existing tests to make the new ones pass.
Investigating or fixing tests that already fail or are flaky.
Refactoring `{subject}` to make it easier to test.
If a new test shows `{subject}` behaving in a way that looks wrong, stop before changing its code: report the input, the actual result and the result you expected, and ask whether to fix it.

If a path of `{subject}` cannot be reached from a test without editing production code (for example a hard-coded path or an unconditional external call), list it with the change that would make it reachable, and ask instead of making the change.
If a new test passes on some runs and fails on others, stop and report the failing output; do not add retries, sleeps or looser assertions to hide it.
If the request is ambiguous about which behaviours to cover, or contradicts what the code shows, stop and ask rather than guessing.

Re-read each changed test file and confirm every behaviour of `{subject}` named in the request has a test that asserts a specific result; run `git status --porcelain` and confirm no production file is listed.
Re-read `{target_path}` and confirm `{subject}` is unchanged.
